World.title: Lee Know Funds Nepal Flood Relief
World.description: Stray Kids member Lee Know donated 100 million won (~$75,000) to World Vision for emergency relief after catastrophic Nepal-Tibet flash floods, JYP Entertainment said Aug. 30. The gift, delivered Aug. 28, is earmarked for food, nutrition, temporary housing, and safe water and sanitation for children and families hit by the disaster. "I hope my small contribution can offer some comfort to those going through difficult times," Lee Know said via JYP, wishing victims and relief workers "a peaceful daily life." He has backed World Vision since 2014 and in 2024 gave another 100 million won to its Global Food Crisis Response, becoming the NGO's youngest Bob Pierce Honor Club member. Last year he donated 200 million won split between Samsung Seoul Hospital patient care and a Goyang cat-rescue group. The K-pop star's latest gift lands as Nepal and Tibet still search for thousands missing after glacier-triggered floods killed hundreds along the border.

USA.title: US deports Afghan to Central Africa
USA.description: The United States on Saturday deported dozens of people to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan man in his early twenties whose brothers collaborated with the U.S. military, lawyer Alma David and Human Rights First said. A U.S. judge had blocked sending him back to Afghanistan over Taliban persecution fears; AP-reviewed court documents said his family received Taliban threats because of that U.S. work. One brother lives in the United States after serving in the Afghan National Army; another, a U.S.-trained pilot, was killed by the Taliban. The flight landed in Bangui with 12 Afghans, eight Iranians, and people from Nepal and Nicaragua, said Savi Arvey of Human Rights First. Advocates say the Trump administration has used often-secret third-country deals to send thousands to about two dozen nations that are not their own — a workaround for people protected from return home. Saturday's flight was the second to CAR since June.

Business.title: Chipotle prank influencer pleads guilty
Business.description: Heston James Cobb, the influencer who posts as "Heston James," pleaded guilty Friday in Arizona to criminal impersonation for posing as an employee during chaotic takeover pranks at businesses in Tempe, a Phoenix suburb, the Associated Press reported. Tempe police arrested him in July 2025 after he and others entered employee-only areas and refused to leave. In one video Cobb wore a Chipotle shirt, told staff he would "clean house," then a group in dark shirts flooded the restaurant; another man mopped a tabletop. Investigators said the videos drew millions of views and potentially large income. Attorney Vicki Lopez declined comment Saturday. Arizona Restaurant Association president Steve Chucri called for "severe" punishment to deter copycats, saying restaurants cannot afford the disruption. University of Tennessee professor Matthew Pittman said the case shows real-world law applies to content: "doing something that is illegal in real life would also be illegal on social."

Technology.title: Abbott freezes Texas Flock camera funding
Technology.description: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ordered state agencies to pause funding for Flock Safety's AI-powered license-plate cameras as privacy backlash and alleged police misuse spread. The Texas Tribune said the order came as it prepared an investigation showing a state agency had put at least $30 million into the Flock network via local-police grants. Spokesman Andrew Mahaleris said most city camera money is federal, and Texas agencies are clarifying state funds cannot be used for Flock. The Motor Vehicle Crime Prevention Authority, with a board mostly appointed by Abbott, has helped install at least 3,200 Flock cameras since 2023, including nearly 1,200 for DPS under a three-year, $15.9 million contract paid from a 2023 $1 auto-insurance fee meant to fight catalytic-converter theft. The cameras log make, model, color and bumper stickers and can be shared nationwide. A Lufkin officer faces 100 counts for allegedly using Flock to surveil 11 people for more than a year.

Entertainment.title: Cruise Green-Flags Thunder Sequel 2028
Entertainment.description: Tom Cruise, 64, hopped a row of potted plants onto a Daytona stage Saturday and told 40 Cup drivers he is bringing Cole Trickle back. Paramount dated the Days of Thunder follow-up for June 2, 2028, nearly 40 years after Tony Scott’s 1990 NASCAR film. Anne Hathaway, 43, will play a team owner and engineer. Cruise posted Instagram video from Daytona International Speedway posing with pregnant Hathaway beside a neon-green race car; she told the camera, “I’m gonna have this baby, and then we’re gonna make this movie.” Jonathan Levine directs a Will Staples script. Cruise produces with Jerry Bruckheimer and Tommy Harper. Variety reports the film will be shot for IMAX and released exclusively in theaters, including Dolby Cinema and 4DX. Cruise waved a green flag hours before NASCAR’s regular-season finale, then sat the drivers’ meeting. He told the room the sequel is about racing’s community, speed, “and all that danger and stuff.”

Sports.title: Hrgovic Stuns Itauma For IBF Belt
Sports.description: Filip Hrgovic stopped 21-year-old Moses Itauma at 2:27 of round nine Saturday at London’s sold-out O2 Arena, taking the vacant IBF heavyweight title and becoming Croatia’s first world heavyweight champion. Itauma entered 14-0 with 12 knockouts, a 9-1 favorite chasing the second-youngest heavyweight belt after Mike Tyson. The Brit dropped 34-year-old Hrgovic (21-1, 16 KOs) in round two and won the early rounds, but had never been past six. A fifth-round uppercut landed flush; Hrgovic walked through it. Itauma emptied his tank in the eighth. In the ninth he was out on his feet; trainer Ben Davison threw in the towel as referee Howard Foster waved it off. Itauma left on a stretcher; promoter Frank Warren cited a late-round leg injury. Hrgovic, who said he had been “outboxed,” told the ring: “I am the present. He is definitely the future.”

Science.title: Roman Telescope Launches Sunday Morning
Science.description: NASA’s $4.3 billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is targeted for 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday, Aug. 30, on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Kennedy Space Center pad 39A. Space Force weather officers put favorable conditions at 60 percent. The 42-foot, 18,000-pound observatory carries a 7.9-foot Hubble-class mirror the National Reconnaissance Office donated after a spy-satellite program was canceled. Bound for Sun-Earth L2, about a million miles from Earth, Roman is designed to scan the sky 1,000 times faster than Hubble. Its 300-megapixel wide-field camera will downlink about 2,500 terabytes over a five-year primary mission, versus Hubble’s 172 terabytes in 30 years. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said it will “give the Earth a new atlas of the universe.” Science chief Niki Fox called it “a sheer powerhouse.” The flagship is launching nine months early and will hunt dark energy, dark matter, and more than 100,000 exoplanets.

Crypto.title: Bitwise Solana ETF Crosses $1 Billion
Crypto.description: Bitwise’s Solana Staking ETF, ticker BSOL, crossed $1 billion in assets under management on Aug. 28, 2026, about 10 months after it listed on Oct. 28, 2025 — the first standalone Solana ETF to hit that mark. As of Aug. 26 it held about 9.33 million SOL, valued near $1.018 billion, more than half of all Solana-focused ETF assets. Crypto Briefing said BSOL captured roughly 79 percent of cumulative net flows, leaving Grayscale’s GSOL and Fidelity’s FSOL far behind. SOL itself is about 60 percent below its all-time high. The fund stakes about 96 percent of holdings for a 5.80 percent net reward passed to shareholders. Spot Solana ETF category volume has topped $13 billion since late 2025. Bitwise called the inflows during a drawdown “an impressive indication of investor conviction.” Concentration is the risk: if BSOL saw big outflows, more than half the category’s SOL could hit the market.

AI.title: AI Turns Bin Moans Into Briefs
AI.description: UK councils, schools, and regulators say AI-drafted complaints are exploding in length and complexity, the BBC reported, with Seoul Economic Daily amplifying the story Aug. 30. Deborah Evans of Lawyers in Local Government said a bin-not-emptied gripe that once fit one side of A4 now runs 19–27 pages packed with case law and Acts of Parliament—often misquoted—forcing staff to loop in lawyers. She estimated handling the surge could require doubling complaint-handling headcount, or else slower replies. Pepe Di'Iasio of the Association of School and College Leaders said parents now file multiple AI-generated complaints that strain teachers. The Information Commissioner's Office and data-protection officers warn AI-assisted FOI requests similarly add "hidden workload" via wrong citations and sprawling asks. Advocates note chatbots help neurodivergent people exercise rights as phone lines give way to email. Some agencies now use AI to crush 50-page filings into one-page replies, while others float word-limit forms that critics call accountability curbs.

Health.title: Ozempic Tied to Rare Vision Loss
Health.description: Rutgers researchers found GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) linked to a small rise in ischemic optic neuropathy—a rare optic-nerve blood-flow failure that can cause sudden, often permanent vision loss—SciTechDaily reported, covering a study in Annals of Internal Medicine. In U.S. adults ages 18–65 with Type 2 diabetes starting diabetes medications, GLP-1 users saw roughly three to four extra cases per 10,000 patients over 18 months. Lead author Chintan Dave said the absolute risk is tiny but clinically serious: "early recognition of symptoms and prompt ophthalmologic evaluation may be especially important" for higher-risk patients, often men or people aged 50–65. Most cases are non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy; about one-third regain some sight within six months, usually with residual field loss rather than total darkness. Authors cautioned underlying health differences may explain the signal and called for more research before proving the drugs cause the risk.
